client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last year. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... find excuses not to go, because being there without her feels unbearable. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that uncertainty is completely okay to bring here. The way you describe being at family gatherings without her sounds genuinely painful, like her absence becomes most visible in the places she used to fill. I'm glad you're here, and I'd love to gently explore what those moments feel like for you — what comes up when you imagine walking into one of those get-togethers?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I picture walking in, the first thing I notice is that I'm already scanning for her — like some part of my brain hasn't fully accepted she won't be there. And then when that registers, it's like this wave of... I don't know, grief mixed with this weird guilt, like I'm somehow betraying her by being there and trying to act normal. It just feels easier to stay home and avoid the whole thing.
therapist: What you're describing — that automatic scan for her, followed by that wave of grief and guilt — shows just how much love is still present in you, even if it's expressing itself in a painful way right now. That guilt you feel about "acting normal" is really worth sitting with, because it sounds like part of you believes that moving through life somehow means leaving her behind — and I'm curious, do you think she would have seen it that way? Avoidance can feel like the kindest thing we can do for ourselves in the short term, but gently, I wonder what it might be costing you over time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, no — she wouldn't have seen it that way. She was the one who always pushed us all to be together, so part of me knows she'd probably be frustrated watching me hide at home. But knowing that doesn't really make it easier to walk through the door, and I guess that's what I don't know how to bridge — like, the logic is there, but the feeling just overrides it completely.
therapist: What you just named is actually one of the most human and universal struggles there is — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel*, and how the heart doesn't always follow the mind's logic, especially in grief. It sounds like there's something tender underneath this, almost like walking through that door makes the loss feel more final, more real — and staying home keeps a kind of protective distance from that. I'm wondering, when you imagine actually going and letting yourself feel whatever comes up, what feels most scary about that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what scares me most is losing control in front of everyone — like, what if I just break down crying at the dinner table and can't stop. My family doesn't really do emotions openly, so I'd probably just make everyone uncomfortable, and then I'd feel guilty about that on top of everything else. It's like there's no version of going where I don't end up feeling worse somehow.
therapist: The way you've laid that out — "there's no version of going where I don't end up feeling worse" — that's a really important thought to notice, because it's essentially a belief that's making the decision for you before you even get there. I'm also struck by how quietly you're carrying all of this, like even talking about it right now feels like something to be contained. What do you think it would actually mean about you if you *did* cry in front of your family?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would mean I'm weak, or that I can't handle things — which is kind of embarrassing to even say out loud because I know that's probably not true. But that's genuinely what it feels like, like crying would be proof that I'm falling apart while everyone else has somehow moved on. And I guess I've always been the one who holds it together in my family, so breaking that would feel like losing some part of my identity too.
therapist: You said something really courageous just now — recognizing that the thought is probably not true, even while it still *feels* completely real — and that gap is exactly where we can do some meaningful work together. I notice you're speaking about all of this quite softly and quickly, like the words are coming out before you can second-guess them, and I wonder if there's something almost exhausting about holding that "strong one" role for so long — like it's a job you never quite got to resign from. What do you think it would feel like to let someone else in your family see that you're struggling too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, the idea of letting someone see that feels almost foreign to me, like I wouldn't even know how to do it without it feeling forced or dramatic. And I'm not sure my family would know how to respond either — they might just get uncomfortable and change the subject, which would honestly feel worse than keeping it to myself. I guess I've been doing this for so long that I'm not even sure who I am in that family if I'm not the one holding everything together.
therapist: That last thing you said — not knowing who you are in your family without that role — feels like it might be the heart of so much of this, and it's a really profound thing to sit with. There's something in how you're speaking about it, quietly and carefully, that makes me wonder if this goes deeper than just grief over your grandmother — like her passing may have also shaken something in how you understand your own place in the world. I'm curious: when did you first start becoming "the one who holds it together," and was that ever really a choice you made, or something that just gradually became expected of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't think it was ever really a choice — it just kind of happened, and honestly my grandmother was a big part of why I could even sustain it, because she was the one person who I felt like actually saw through it. She'd check in on me quietly, away from everyone else, and I never had to explain myself to her. So maybe losing her also means losing the one person who knew I was struggling underneath all of that, and now it's like I'm completely invisible in that way.
therapist: What you just shared feels like the truest thing yet — that losing her wasn't just losing your grandmother, but losing the one witness to your real self, the person who made it safe to not have to perform. And I notice as you're saying this, your voice has gone very quiet and quick, like the words are slipping out before you can quite hold them back — which makes me wonder if even *saying this out loud* is bringing up something that's been sitting very deep for a long time. Can you stay with that feeling for a moment — what's it like to have named it just now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: It's strange — saying it out loud made it feel more real, and now I'm sitting here trying not to cry, which is kind of ironic given everything we just talked about. I think I've known this somewhere underneath for a while, but I've been so busy just getting through each day that I never let myself actually look at it. It's a relief in a weird way, but also really lonely, like naming it makes the loss feel even bigger somehow.
therapist: The irony isn't lost on me either — that in a session about being afraid to cry, you're sitting here on the edge of tears, and that actually feels like something really important happening, not something to push away. What you're describing, that strange mix of relief and loneliness, makes complete sense — naming a truth can feel like finally setting down a heavy bag, while also making you fully aware of how long you've been carrying it. You don't have to hold it together here, with me — this is actually one of the few places where letting it be as big as it is might be exactly the right thing to do.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and part of me wants to just let go, but there's still this reflex that kicks in where I kind of pull back from it. It's like even here, with someone I'm supposed to be able to be honest with, I'm monitoring myself and making sure I don't go too far. I'm not sure how you actually unlearn something like that — it feels so automatic that I don't know where I'd even start.
therapist: That reflex you're describing — the self-monitoring, the pulling back just before you go "too far" — is actually the pattern we've been circling around this whole conversation, and the fact that you can *see* it happening in real time is genuinely significant. It makes sense that it feels automatic, because it was learned over a long time as a way to stay safe, but what gets learned can, slowly and gently, be unlearned — and noticing it, like you just did, is actually the first step. I'm wondering, even right now, what would happen if you just let yourself not pull back for one moment — what feels like it's on the other side of that reflex?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what's on the other side is just... really deep sadness, and maybe the fear that once I start feeling it fully, it won't stop — like it'll just swallow me whole. I know that probably sounds irrational, but grief this size feels dangerous somehow, like it's been contained for a reason. I guess I don't fully trust yet that it's safe to let it out, even here.
therapist: What you're describing doesn't sound irrational at all — that fear that grief will be bottomless, that once the door opens it won't close again, is one of the most common and understandable fears people carry, especially when they've been containing something this big for this long. The truth that CBT and grief work both point to is that feelings, even enormous ones, do move through us when we let them — they're not actually bottomless, even when they feel that way. You don't have to trust that fully yet, but I want you to know that building that trust, at whatever pace feels safe, is exactly what this space is for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
